answer: He has mistaken his refusal for power. Most men refuse things: they refuse their illness, their losses, the indifference of others. But refusing isn't the same as overcoming. He stands there against an unmoving thing and declares himself king over it simply because he won't look away. That kind of dignity is a form of revolt, yes, but it's a blind one. It refuses to see that something real is happening and insists instead that it should go another way. There is something almost touching about it—his utter refusal to submit is honest—but there is also something dangerous. A man who decides that reality must bend to him cannot endure when it doesn't, and usually ends up breaking himself trying to force it. His letters are not quite madness yet, but they are close to a kind of holy obstinacy that makes him unable to live with other people, whose lives and deaths are equally stubborn.
